opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the most interesting challenges with Genie. We learn the action space without any action labels. We train on unlabeled video from the internet, like 2D platformer gameplay, and the model has to infer a set of latent actions that explain what changes from one frame to the next. Nobody tells it, "this is the character, this is what you control."

So the question is: when you pick one of those latent actions, what actually moves? Ideally it's the playable character, because in that data the character is usually what's being driven by someone's inputs. But the model doesn't know that a priori. There's a lot going on in a frame. The background might scroll, enemies move, there's parallax and other effects. Any of those could plausibly be "the thing that changed."

What helps is that we keep the latent action space very small, just a handful of discrete actions. That bottleneck forces the model to explain the most consistent, controllable source of variation with those few codes. Things that happen regardless of what the player does, like background motion, get absorbed by the dynamics model as just how the world evolves. What's left over, the part that varies in a way that needs extra information, tends to be the agent. So we got a nice emergent result: the latent actions often did correspond to things like moving left, moving right or jumping, and they mostly applied to the character.

It's not guaranteed, though. Sometimes an action affects something you didn't intend, or the semantics aren't perfectly consistent across very different environments. If an image has no clear protagonist, or it's ambiguous what should be controllable, the model has to make a guess. So I think of it as a problem of identifiability: from observation alone, which changes are caused by an agent and which are just the world? Video gives you a strong signal, but not a perfect one.

Going forward, I think there's a lot of room to make that more reliable. You could use a small amount of labeled data to ground the latent actions, or give the model more explicit cues about what the agent is. Scale and more diverse data also help the model learn what "being an agent" looks like across many settings. But I find it fascinating that this much controllability emerges at all, just from watching.

r001.rationale: The response says latent actions often correspond to controlling the character, but that this is not guaranteed and may be inconsistent. It does not state that success with one action makes all actions control the same part.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really one of the central challenges with Genie, and it comes down to the fact that we're learning the action space in a completely unsupervised way. We're training on videos from the internet, and those videos don't come with action labels. So we introduce this latent action model, where the model has to infer, between two consecutive frames, what was the thing that changed, and compress that into a small discrete set of codes.

The difficulty is that a video has a lot going on in it. In a platformer, say, the character moves, but the camera also pans, enemies move, background elements animate, clouds drift by. The model has no built-in notion that the character is the thing we care about. From its perspective, it's just trying to explain the difference between frame t and frame t plus one as efficiently as it can. So what ends up getting captured in the latent action is whatever is the most predictable, most consistent source of change across the dataset.

What we found is that, because the latent action space is so small, something like eight actions, there's a strong pressure on the model to be really economical. It can't afford to encode everything, so it tends to latch onto the dominant controllable factor. And in a lot of video game footage, that does turn out to be the player, because the player is what moves most consistently and in ways that are hard to predict from the frames alone. So in that sense the bottleneck is actually doing a lot of work for us.

But it's not guaranteed. In some domains the actions pick up on camera motion, or they entangle the agent's motion with the camera. And when you then try to use Genie as a controllable simulator, that's a real limitation, because you'd like to say, this action means move right, and have it mean that regardless of what else is happening in the scene. We saw this when we looked at the robotics data too. The latent actions were often quite consistent, which was exciting, but you can't always just read off what a given code is going to do until you try it.

So the way I think about it is, controllability emerges rather than being specified. The model discovers what's controllable, and we get a lot of it for free from the data distribution and the bottleneck, but closing the gap between what it finds controllable and what we want to control is really one of the big open questions for this line of work.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that all actions control the same intended part once one action does. It instead says control is not guaranteed and latent actions may capture camera motion or entangle factors.

astra-6.text:
I think the tricky thing is that Genie is learning from video, where you can see what changes, but you don’t necessarily know what caused that change. You don’t have the actions that someone took. So it has to infer a representation of actions and figure out which changes those actions should control.

If there’s a character moving through a scene, you might want to control that character. But there can also be camera motion or other things moving in the background. Just from observing the video, it’s not always clear which of those is the thing you intend to control. So learning something that produces changes in the environment is one challenge; making those changes line up with what a person means by an action is another.

r001.rationale: The response discusses identifying the intended controllable part, but does not say that once one action controls it, all Genie actions control that same part.

sol-6.1.text: I think the difficulty is that Genie has to infer what’s controllable just from watching video. It doesn’t have the actions that produced those changes, so it has to discover that relationship for itself. And there can be lots of things moving in a scene—the character, the camera, objects in the background. How does it know which of those you intend to control? Learning something that predicts how the scene changes isn’t necessarily the same as learning the particular control interface a person wants.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how Genie must infer which scene elements are controllable and intended, but does not say that once one action controls the intended part, all actions control that same part.
